Senses.Note: Exact count: 47 hits in 33 allowlisted texts. Family research covered the woodcutter, rotted axe/handle, chess game, lost road, Lanke person, and the separate Mount Lanke place-name. The allusion and the mountain are different referents and are split.

Occurrences.Kwic: 局罷不知何處去空山惆悵爛柯人
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Fang'an Xian, explicitly credited in (禪宗頌古聯珠通集) (Linked Pearls Collection of Chan Verse Comments), writes this verse on the Lanke man.

Occurrences.Kwic: 爛柯樵子疑無路，挂樹壺公玅有家。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuan'an Feng, in (遠菴僼禪師語錄) (Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yuan'an Feng), pairs the Lanke woodcutter with the gourd master.

Occurrences.Kwic: 謾支折脚鐺，拈起爛柯斧，饑將脫粟炊，衣裁荷葉補。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source text (五燈全書(第34卷-第120卷)): Yongjue Yuanxian, in (五燈全書)(第34卷-第120卷) (Complete Book of the Five Lamps), lists the Lanke axe beside a broken-legged pot.

Occurrences.Kwic: 斧爛柯銷局未闌天風吹鶴下瑤壇
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhongfeng Mingben, in (天目中峰廣錄) (Extensive Record of Zhongfeng at Tianmu), says the handle is gone while the game remains unfinished.

Occurrences.Kwic: 已有爛柯樵子本傳。前頌雪峯末後句。亦有挂樹壺公本傳
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Wansong Xingxiu, in (萬松老人評唱天童覺和尚頌古從容庵錄) (Wansong's Commentary in the Book of Serenity), identifies the original Lanke woodcutter account.

Senses.Explanation: The rotted axe handle is the records’ time-lapse allusion: a woodcutter watches an immortal chess game and returns after his handle has decayed. The Chan corpus does not usually retell that background in full; it repeatedly names its visible pieces. Fang'an Xian says that when the game ends no one knows where to go, leaving “the Lanke man” sorrowful in the empty mountain (局罷不知何處去，空山惆悵爛柯人). Yuan'an Feng repeats, “the Lanke woodcutter doubts there is a road” (爛柯樵子疑無路). Yongjue Yuanxian lists taking up “the Lanke axe” beside propping a broken-legged pot, while Zhongfeng Mingben says the axe handle has rotted and vanished but the game is not yet finished. Wansong Xingxiu explicitly says that an earlier verse already has the original account of the Lanke woodcutter (已有爛柯樵子本傳). The Zen-specific bend is this repeated use of the rotted handle, woodcutter, unfinished game, and lost road as a compact allusion in case verse and formal speech. The outside story remains an inherited historical lead except where the Chan text names these elements directly.

Senses.Note: Mount Lanke occurs as a compound place-name in several allowlisted texts. One exact place witness is sufficient to establish the distinct referent; the entry makes no claim about the mountain's outside history.

Occurrences.Kwic: 爛柯山雨似傾盆，龜嶺峯額頭汗出
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Xiatang Huiyuan, in (瞎堂慧遠禪師廣錄) (Extensive Record of Chan Master Xiatang Huiyuan), names rain on Mount Lanke.

Senses.Explanation: The same graph pair also forms the proper place-name Mount Lanke. Xiatang Huiyuan says that rain on Mount Lanke pours like a basin while Turtle Ridge's forehead sweats. This geographic referent is not the rotted axe handle or its woodcutter, even though the place-name inherits the same graphs; it therefore has its own sense.
